course: Daily Milk Sales: Dairy Herd System

lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body:
Milk is a perishable product. In warm African conditions, fresh milk can spoil in as little as 2 hours if not handled properly. When milk spoils, you lose money, and your customers may get sick. This module teaches you how to handle milk from the moment it leaves the cow until it reaches the customer, using simple tools and methods that work in rural and peri-urban settings.

Why is milk handling so important? First, milk is a perfect food for bacteria. Bacteria double every 20 minutes in warm milk. If you milk a cow at 6 AM and leave the bucket in the sun, by 8 AM the milk may already be sour. Second, customers pay for quality. Clean, cool milk tastes better and lasts longer. Third, your reputation matters. If you sell spoiled milk, you lose customers and your business fails.

The cold chain is the system that keeps milk cool from farm to customer. It includes clean containers, rapid cooling, and a cold storage method like a fridge, freezer, or insulated box with ice. In many parts of Africa, electricity is unreliable, so we use alternatives like solar-powered coolers, charcoal coolers, or simply selling milk quickly. The goal is to keep milk below 4Â°C (39Â°F) to slow bacterial growth.

In this module, you will learn the tools you need, the step-by-step method for handling milk, common mistakes and how to fix them, safety practices, and you will do a practical exercise. By the end, you will be able to set up a simple cold chain that protects your milk and your income. Remember: every hour counts. The faster you cool milk, the longer it lasts and the more you can sell.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body:
To handle milk properly, you need the right tools. These are affordable and can be found in local markets or made by a craftsman. Start with a stainless steel or aluminum milking bucket. Avoid plastic buckets that scratch easily because scratches hide bacteria. A 10-liter bucket with a lid costs about $10-15. You also need a clean cloth or filter to strain milk. Use a fine mesh strainer or a clean cotton cloth boiled and dried in the sun.

For cooling, you need a thermometer to check milk temperature. A simple dial thermometer costs $3-5. You also need a cooling container. If you have electricity, a refrigerator is best. If not, use an insulated cooler box (like a picnic cooler) and ice packs. You can freeze water in plastic bottles to use as ice packs. A 50-liter cooler box costs $30-50. For larger scale, consider a solar-powered milk cooler, which is expensive but effective.

For storage and transport, use food-grade plastic or stainless steel cans with tight lids. Never use jerrycans that held chemicals or fuel. For cleaning, you need hot water, dish soap, and a brush. A bottle brush helps clean inside narrow containers. Also keep a clean towel or paper towels for drying. Drying is important because bacteria need moisture.

For testing milk quality, you can use a lactometer to check for added water, and a simple alcohol test to check freshness. The alcohol test: mix equal parts milk and 70% alcohol; if it curdles, the milk is not fresh. These tools are optional but helpful. Finally, keep a record book to note milking times, temperatures, and sales. This helps you track problems and improve. All these tools together can cost under $100, which is a small investment for a dairy business.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body:
Follow these steps every time you handle milk. Step 1: Prepare before milking. Wash your hands with soap and water. Clean the cow's udder with a clean cloth and warm water. Use a separate cloth for each cow to prevent spreading bacteria. Step 2: Milk into a clean, sanitized bucket. Discard the first few squirts because they contain high bacteria. Milk quickly but gently. Step 3: Strain the milk immediately. Pour milk through a clean cloth or strainer into another clean container. This removes dirt, hair, and some bacteria.

Step 4: Cool the milk fast. Within 30 minutes of milking, place the milk container in a cool water bath or in a refrigerator. If using a cooler box, put ice packs around the container. Stir the milk gently to cool evenly. Aim to bring milk to 4Â°C within 2 hours. Use a thermometer to check. Step 5: Store milk at 4Â°C or below. Keep it covered. Do not open the cooler or fridge often. If using a cooler box, replace ice packs every 12 hours. Step 6: Transport milk cold. Use an insulated bag or cooler box. Keep it out of the sun. If delivering by bicycle or motorbike, wrap the cooler in a blanket for extra insulation.

Step 7: Sell or process quickly. Milk stored at 4Â°C can last 2-3 days. If you cannot sell within that time, process it into yogurt, cheese, or butter. Step 8: Clean all equipment immediately after use. Wash with hot water and soap, rinse with clean water, and sanitize with boiling water or a bleach solution (1 tablespoon bleach per 1 liter water). Dry in the sun. Step 9: Record everything. Note the time of milking, cooling, and temperature. This helps you find where problems happen. Following these steps reduces spoilage and keeps customers happy.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body:
Mistake 1: Using dirty containers. Fix: Always wash and sanitize buckets, cans, and lids before use. If you can see dirt or smell sourness, wash again. Mistake 2: Leaving milk in the sun. Fix: Keep milk in the shade and cool it immediately. Even 30 minutes in direct sun can spoil milk. Mistake 3: Not cooling fast enough. Fix: Use a water bath with ice or cold water. Stir the milk. If you have no ice, use a wet cloth wrapped around the container and place it in a breeze. Evaporation cools the milk.

Mistake 4: Mixing warm milk with cold milk. Fix: Never add fresh warm milk to already cooled milk. This warms the whole batch and speeds spoilage. Cool new milk first, then add. Mistake 5: Using the same cloth for multiple cows. Fix: Use a separate clean cloth for each cow's udder. Wash cloths after each milking. Mistake 6: Not testing milk quality. Fix: Do a simple alcohol test or taste test. If milk tastes sour or bitter, do not sell it. Use it for cooking or feed it to calves after boiling.

Mistake 7: Storing milk in open containers. Fix: Always cover milk tightly. Open milk absorbs smells and bacteria from the air. Mistake 8: Overloading the cooler. Fix: Do not pack too many containers in one cooler. Air must circulate for even cooling. Leave some space. Mistake 9: Ignoring temperature. Fix: Use a thermometer. If milk is above 4Â°C, add more ice or move to a colder place. Mistake 10: Selling milk without proper records. Fix: Keep a simple notebook. Write down milking time, cooling time, temperature, and sales. This helps you identify patterns and improve.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body:
Safety is about protecting both you and your customers. Always wash your hands with soap before and after handling milk. Wear clean clothes and tie back long hair. If you are sick, especially with diarrhea or vomiting, do not handle milk. You can spread harmful bacteria. Keep animals away from the milking area. Flies and rodents carry bacteria. Use screens or nets if possible.

Use only potable water for cleaning. If water is not safe to drink, boil it first. Sanitize equipment with a bleach solution: 1 tablespoon of household bleach per 1 liter of water. Soak for 2 minutes, then rinse with boiled water. Do not use too much bleach because it can leave harmful residues. Store cleaning chemicals away from milk containers.

Best practice: Cool milk to 4Â°C within 2 hours. Keep a thermometer in the cooler to monitor temperature. If temperature rises above 7Â°C, the milk is at risk. Discard milk that has been above 10Â°C for more than 2 hours. Never sell milk from a sick cow or cow on antibiotics. Antibiotics can pass into milk and cause allergic reactions or antibiotic resistance in people. Follow withdrawal times given by a vet.

Label milk containers with the date and time of milking. Use the oldest milk first. If you sell to a milk collection center, follow their quality standards. They may test for antibiotics, water, and bacteria. Keep records of all tests. Train anyone who helps you. A single mistake by a worker can spoil a whole batch. Finally, have a plan for power cuts. Keep ice packs frozen and a backup cooler. In case of a long power cut, sell milk quickly or process it into yogurt. Safety and best practice protect your business and your community.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body:
Now it is time to practice. This exercise will help you set up a simple cold chain for your milk. You will need: a milking bucket, a strainer, a thermometer, a cooler box, and ice packs (or frozen water bottles). If you do not have a cooler box, use a large pot and a wet cloth. Do this exercise over two days.

Day 1: Morning milking. Record the time you start milking. Wash your hands and the cow's udder. Milk into a clean bucket. Strain the milk into a clean container. Immediately check the temperature. It should be around 37Â°C (body temperature). Now cool it. Place the container in a water bath with cold water and ice. Stir gently every 5 minutes. Check the temperature every 15 minutes. Record how long it takes to reach 4Â°C. If you have no ice, wrap the container in a wet cloth and place it in a shaded, breezy spot. Record the temperature every 15 minutes for 2 hours. Note the final temperature.

Day 2: Storage and transport test. Take the cooled milk from Day 1 (if still cold). If it is still at 4Â°C, it is good. If it smells sour, discard. Now simulate transport: put the milk container in your cooler box with ice packs. Close the lid. Leave it for 2 hours. Then check the temperature. It should still be below 7Â°C. If it is higher, add more ice packs or improve insulation. Write down your observations.

Finally, calculate your results. How long did it take to cool milk? How much ice did you use? What could you improve? Share your findings with a fellow farmer. This exercise teaches you the real challenges of the cold chain. Repeat it until you can consistently cool milk to 4Â°C within 2 hours. With practice, you will protect your milk and increase your sales.

quiz.q: Why is milk handling important for a dairy business?
options: A) It makes milk taste better.
B) It prevents spoilage and keeps customers safe.
C) It increases the fat content of milk.
D) It reduces the need for refrigeration.
quiz.explanation: Proper handling prevents bacterial growth and spoilage, ensuring safe milk and satisfied customers.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature to store fresh milk?
quiz.explanation: Milk should be kept at 4Â°C or below to slow bacterial growth.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for milking to avoid bacteria?
quiz.explanation: Stainless steel is easy to clean and does not scratch, reducing bacterial hiding places.

quiz.q: How often do bacteria double in warm milk?
quiz.explanation: Bacteria can double every 20 minutes in warm milk, leading to rapid spoilage.

quiz.q: What is the first step before milking?
options: B) Wash hands and clean the udder
quiz.explanation: Clean hands and udder prevent bacteria from entering the milk.

quiz.q: Why should you discard the first few squirts of milk?
quiz.explanation: The first squirts contain high levels of bacteria from the teat canal.

quiz.q: How soon should milk be cooled after milking?
quiz.explanation: Cooling within 30 minutes slows bacterial growth quickly.

quiz.q: What is a simple test for milk freshness?
quiz.explanation: The alcohol test shows if milk is fresh; curdling indicates spoilage.

quiz.q: What should you use to sanitize milk containers?
quiz.explanation: A diluted bleach solution kills bacteria on containers.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake in milk handling?
options: C) Storing milk in the shade
quiz.explanation: Dirty containers introduce bacteria and cause spoilage.

quiz.q: How can you cool milk without electricity?
options: A) Put it in the sun
B) Use a water bath with ice
quiz.explanation: A water bath with ice rapidly lowers milk temperature.

quiz.q: Why should you not mix warm milk with cold milk?
options: B) It warms the whole batch and speeds spoilage
quiz.explanation: Mixing warm milk raises the temperature of the cold milk, promoting bacterial growth.

quiz.q: What is a sign that milk is spoiled?
quiz.explanation: Sour smell or taste indicates bacterial growth and spoilage.

quiz.q: How often should you replace ice packs in a cooler box?
quiz.explanation: Ice packs typically need replacement every 12 hours to maintain cold temperature.

quiz.q: What should you do if milk temperature rises above 7Â°C?
options: B) Add more ice or move to a colder place
quiz.explanation: Act immediately to cool milk back to safe temperature.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep records in milk handling?
options: A) To track temperatures and improve
quiz.explanation: Records help identify problems and improve handling practices.

quiz.q: What should you do if you are sick with diarrhea?
quiz.explanation: Sick people can spread harmful bacteria to milk.

quiz.q: What is a safe way to clean water for milk handling?
quiz.explanation: Boiling kills pathogens in water used for cleaning.

quiz.q: Why should you not sell milk from a cow on antibiotics?
options: B) It can cause antibiotic resistance in people
quiz.explanation: Antibiotic residues can lead to resistance and allergic reactions.

quiz.q: What is a good alternative to a refrigerator for cooling milk?
quiz.explanation: Solar coolers are effective where electricity is unreliable.

quiz.q: How long can milk last at 4Â°C?
quiz.explanation: Properly cooled milk can last 2-3 days.

quiz.q: What should you do with milk that has been above 10Â°C for 2 hours?
quiz.explanation: Milk above 10Â°C for 2 hours is unsafe and should be discarded.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of straining milk?
options: A) To remove dirt and hair
quiz.explanation: Straining removes physical contaminants and some bacteria.

quiz.q: How can you keep milk cool during transport?
options: B) Put it in the sun
quiz.explanation: Insulated bags maintain cold temperature during transport.

quiz.q: What is a sign of good milk quality?
options: B) Sweet smell and smooth texture
quiz.explanation: Fresh milk has a sweet smell and smooth texture.

quiz.q: Why should you label milk containers with date and time?
options: A) To use oldest milk first
quiz.explanation: Labeling helps with stock rotation and ensures freshness.

quiz.q: What should you do if you have a power cut?
quiz.explanation: Sell or process milk quickly to prevent spoilage during power cuts.

quiz.q: What is a practical exercise for learning milk handling?
options: A) Cooling milk and recording temperatures
quiz.explanation: Hands-on practice with cooling and recording builds skills.

quiz.q: How can you tell if milk is properly cooled?
quiz.explanation: A thermometer gives an accurate temperature reading.

quiz.q: What is the best way to dry milk containers after washing?
quiz.explanation: Sun drying kills bacteria and removes moisture.
